sections.title: Purposeful Movement
sections.content: How you move on stage is as important as what you say. Nervous pacing distracts the audience. Purposeful movement anchors your arguments physically and keeps the audience engaged.
bullets: Nervous pacing = rocking, shifting weight, walking in circles
Purposeful movement = stepping deliberately to a new spot for a new idea
Your physical position should mark transitions in your speech

sections.title: The 3-Point Anchor System
sections.content: For a three-argument speech, use three positions on stage: left for argument 1, center for argument 2, right for argument 3. Return to center for conclusion.
bullets: Position 1 (left): Open with your first argument
Position 2 (center): Transition to your second argument
Return to center: Conclude and summarize

sections.title: Stage Map
sections.content: A stage map for a three-point debate speech:
sections.good:
[Left] Argument 1: Economic impact
[Center] Argument 2: Social impact
[Right] Argument 3: Environmental impact
[Center] Conclusion
sections.explanation: Each movement marks a clear transition. Return to center for closure.

sections.instruction: When is the best time to physically step to a new position on stage?
options: In the middle of a sentence for emphasis
When transitioning to a new argument or main point
As often as possible to show energy
sections.feedback: Move when you transition to a new point. This signals a content shift visually.

sections.q: Why does the 3-Point Anchor System make a speech more memorable?
options: It creates a physical map that reinforces your argument structure
sections.explain: Linking each argument to a physical position creates spatial memory for the audience.

sections.statement: Standing perfectly still during your entire speech projects the most confidence.
sections.feedback: Complete stillness can look frozen. Controlled movement shows you own the space.

sections.sentence: The {0}-Point Anchor System uses different stage positions for each main argument.
sections.instruction: Fill in the number of anchor positions.
sections.feedback: A three-position system works naturally for three-argument speeches.

sections.scenario: You are delivering a 5-minute speech with three main arguments. The room is large, and the audience seems distracted. You notice people checking their phones during your first argument.
sections.question: What should you do to regain the audience's attention?
options: Speak louder and faster to push through the content
Use the 3-Point Anchor System: step to a new position for your second argument, pause, and make eye contact before continuing
Ignore the distractions and keep going as planned
Ask the audience to pay attention
sections.feedback: Purposeful movement to a new position signals a transition. Combined with a pause and eye contact, it forces the audience to refocus on you.

questions.statement: Return to center stage for your conclusion after using the 3-Point Anchor System.
questions.feedback: Returning to center signals the end of the journey and creates closure.
